global.headline: IRAN DECLARES "FULL-SCALE WAR" AS HOUTHIS BLOCKADE SAUDI SHIPPING AND MOJTABA KHAMENEI BREAKS SILENCE TO DEMAND "SACRED UNITY"
summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian declared Monday that Iran and the US are now fighting a "full-scale war," as CENTCOM extended its bombing campaign into a ninth consecutive night — hitting the north-western city of Tabriz (believed to house underground missile bases) and the port of Bushehr, home to Iran's only operating civilian nuclear plant — before explosions were reported early Monday in Hormozgan province (Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, and the Bemani district near the Strait of Hormuz) as strikes continued into a new night. The confirmed US military death toll held at 17 after Saturday's fatal Iraq drone-ordnance incident; no new US fatality was confirmed within this window. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday Washington remained "open to diplomacy," adding "if that door opens, we'll be happy to see it open" — though "their behaviour has to change in order for ours to change" — while Tehran foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said mediators had passed messages between the two sides without giving details.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated sharply Sunday, declaring a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and vowing to close the Bab el-Mandeb strait — through which roughly 12% of world trade passes — in retaliation for what they call Riyadh's decade-long "blockade" of Sana'a and the collapse of their four-year truce after last week's Sanaa/Abha airport strikes. A Houthi spokesperson called it "an eye for an eye"; the Saudi-led coalition said it had taken steps to protect Red Sea shipping. The move widens the war's economic footprint far beyond the already near-frozen Strait of Hormuz.

In his first public remarks since being confirmed Supreme Leader in March, Mojtaba Khamenei issued a written statement Saturday — he has still not appeared in person or been heard from directly — accusing Washington of "bullying, hegemony and savagery" and vowing to teach the US "unforgettable lessons," while separately urging Iranians to preserve "sacred unity" and warning critics of the leadership not to "cause a fracture in national unity and social cohesion." The statement obliquely acknowledges, without directly rebutting, the hardliner "coup" accusations levelled at acting leaders Ghalibaf, Pezeshkian and Araghchi (18-19 Jul); officials have since worked to project a united front. Separately, Mohsen Rezaei's ultimatum — that continued US strikes would push Iran to "offensive and complete destruction" within "two or three days" — expired around 19-20 Jul with no confirmed shift in Iranian tactics; his authority to set such a deadline remains unclear given his advisory-only role.
global.geopolitical: Pezeshkian's "full-scale war" framing, the Houthis' new Red Sea blockade and Mojtaba Khamenei's carefully hedged unity message together suggest an Iranian state stretching to manage three fronts at once — the US bombing campaign, an increasingly independent-acting IRGC/Houthi axis, and internal elite infighting over who actually controls the war — while Rubio keeps a diplomatic door notionally open with no sign either side is walking through it.
global.socioeconomic: A second maritime chokepoint under direct threat — Bab el-Mandeb alongside an already near-frozen Hormuz — compounds the shipping-insurance and freight-cost shock already rippling through the Asian trade lanes Singapore depends on, adding to the same oil-price channel already visible in record COE premiums and the record Q3 electricity tariff.

global.headline: GOLDEN LEO DEATH TOLL DOUBLES TO 10 AS UKRAINE HITS MOSCOW REGION WITH RECORD 400-DRONE BARRAGE
summary: The death toll from Russia's cruise-missile strike on the Golden Leo — the Guinea-Bissau-flagged grain carrier hit off Odesa on 19 July — rose from 5 to 10 as Ukrainian officials confirmed nine of its Indian and Syrian crew and one harbour pilot were killed, with eight crew rescued; Ukraine's navy called it the deadliest single attack in the Black Sea's weeks-long flare-up.

Ukraine retaliated overnight with what Moscow's own mayor Sergei Sobyanin called one of the war's largest drone raids on the Russian capital region — Kyiv launched more than 400 drones, of which Russia claimed 85 were shot down approaching Moscow. Strikes hit an oil depot at Podolsk (sending black smoke over the city), a Wildberries fulfilment centre at Kolyedino, and warehouses at the Yuzhnye Vorota logistics park in Belye Stolby, all roughly 25-40km south of the Kremlin; President Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck logistics facilities and an oil depot more than 400km inside Russia. It follows the 41-missile, 125-drone barrage that hit Kyiv on 19 July (1 killed, 16 injured), which Ukraine's air force had called the largest ballistic-missile barrage of the war.
global.geopolitical: Ukraine's ability to mount a 400-drone strike on the Russian capital's own logistics and fuel infrastructure, not just border regions, signals a deep-strike capability that keeps expanding even as Kyiv absorbs record missile barrages of its own, keeping both sides locked in an escalating exchange with no ceasefire framework in sight.
global.socioeconomic: A doubled Black Sea grain-ship death toll and a fuel-depot strike deep inside Russia both feed the same global shipping-insurance and commodity-cost pressures already elevated by the separate Iran-driven oil shock, compounding cost risk for import-dependent Asian economies including Singapore.

global.headline: INDIAN POLICE FIRE TEAR GAS AS 10,000+ "COCKROACH MOVEMENT" PROTESTERS MARCH ON PARLIAMENT
summary: Police fired tear gas and used baton charges against more than 10,000 protesters from India's youth-led "Cockroach Janta Party" movement as they marched toward Parliament in New Delhi on Monday, demanding the education minister's resignation and a crackdown on corruption after a string of exam-system scandals — leaked papers, technical glitches and cancelled tests. Numbers swelled after Saturday's forcible hospitalisation of 59-year-old activist and engineer Sonam Wangchuk, who had been on hunger strike for three weeks in solidarity with the movement; protesters have occupied New Delhi's Jantar Mantar area and dozens have been arrested.
The march, which defied a Delhi lockdown, was reportedly larger than organisers had expected.
global.geopolitical: A youth movement large and organised enough to defy a lockdown and force a violent police response over exam-system integrity, rather than a narrower economic or communal grievance, signals a broader trust deficit in Indian public institutions that could sharpen into a wider anti-corruption platform if the movement keeps growing.
global.socioeconomic: Recurring exam-system failures feeding mass protest reflect real stakes for India's enormous youth population competing for a limited number of public-sector and university placements — a structural pressure point that keeps recurring regardless of which minister holds the portfolio.

global.headline: TRUMP FORMALLY IMPOSES 50% TARIFF ON CANADIAN GOODS OVER AUTOS, ALCOHOL AND DAIRY DISPUTE
summary: President Trump invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act — which allows tariffs of up to 50% without congressional approval where a trading partner is found to discriminate against US goods — to impose new 50% duties on roughly US$20 billion (S$26.4 billion) of Canadian imports including electrical equipment, machinery, milk and cream, hockey equipment and alcohol, accusing Ottawa of unfairly discriminating against American autos, alcohol and dairy. Energy, potash, fish, critical minerals and goods already covered by separate auto/steel tariffs are exempt; the order takes effect in 30 days.

The formal order is distinct from, and comes on top of, Trump's still-unresolved 17 July threat to add Canadian wildfire-smoke pollution costs to existing tariffs after smoke from 900+ active fires blanketed northern US states — that specific smoke-cost surcharge has not yet been formalised, but the two disputes now compound each other in an already-fraught trade relationship with America's second-largest trading partner.
global.geopolitical: A second, separate tariff front against a G7 neighbour and long-standing security ally, on top of the still-live wildfire-smoke dispute, signals Washington's willingness to escalate economic pressure on allies even while stretched by an active Middle East war, testing how much friction Ottawa absorbs before retaliating.
global.socioeconomic: Formalised duties on autos, alcohol and dairy sit alongside Canada's pre-existing 10% Section 122 tariff exposure and add fresh uncertainty to North American supply chains; Singapore's direct exposure is limited, but it is a fresh data point for a global trade environment already strained by tariff-driven cost pressure feeding into inflation readings MAS will weigh at its next policy review.

global.headline: HAMAS NAMES KHALIL AL-HAYYA AS NEW OVERALL LEADER, SUCCEEDING SINWAR
summary: Hamas named Khalil al-Hayya, 66, as its new overall leader on Monday after he won an internal run-off vote against former political chief Khaled Meshaal, succeeding Yahya Sinwar (killed by Israeli forces in October 2024). Al-Hayya, one of five members of Hamas's leadership council, has led the movement's Gaza operations from exile and was its chief negotiator during the October 2025 ceasefire talks; four of his children have been killed in Israeli strikes over the course of the war.

Al-Hayya is widely seen as representing Hamas's harder-line faction, continuing the political line of the late Ismail Haniyeh and Sinwar rather than a more conciliatory approach; his selection comes as Gaza's post-war governance handoff remains stalled — the Emergency Committee dissolved 6 July with its successor still based outside Gaza pending Israeli objections — and as the nominal ceasefire continues to be violated on both sides.
global.geopolitical: Choosing a hardline continuity candidate over Meshaal, seen as more open to diplomatic engagement, narrows the space for the kind of compromises a durable Gaza governance handoff would require, at a moment Israel's own far-right is separately floating Gaza resettlement plans.
global.socioeconomic: A harder-line Hamas leadership makes near-term progress on Gaza reconstruction financing and donor-conference planning less likely, prolonging the humanitarian and economic stagnation that has weighed on regional trade and aid flows since the war began.

singapore.headline: SENIOR MINISTER FAISHAL IBRAHIM RESIGNS OVER "LAPSE OF JUDGMENT" IN CONDUCT WITH A WOMAN
summary: Associate Professor Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim resigned Monday as Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs, Acting Minister-in-Charge of Muslim Affairs, MP for Kembangan (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights GRC) and PAP member, after the Prime Minister's Office received a complaint about a month ago from a woman regarding her interactions with him. Both Faishal and the woman made harassment allegations against each other; police investigated and found no criminal offence on either side. In a statement, PM Lawrence Wong said Faishal "accepted that his conduct fell short of these standards" and tendered his resignation; Faishal said there had been "no physical relationship" and he had not intended the interactions — mostly online messages and meetings on the sidelines of public events — to develop into one, thanking his wife for standing by him.

No by-election will be called: Minister for National Development Desmond Lee said the remaining four Marine Parade-Braddell Heights GRC MPs will continue serving the Kembangan ward together. Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad has been appointed Acting Minister-in-Charge of Muslim Affairs. The resignation opens a second unfilled Senior Minister of State-level vacancy alongside the Manpower and Health SMS roles that have sat vacant since June.
singapore.geopolitical: A resignation resolved within roughly a month of the complaint reaching the PMO, with a police investigation, a public PM statement and no by-election drama, is itself a data point on how Singapore's political system handles this kind of conduct lapse compared with more protracted scandals elsewhere this month (the Tate brothers, Spahn's CDU resignation) — swift, low-drama, and off the front pages within a single news day.
singapore.socioeconomic: A second Senior Minister of State-level vacancy compounds the still-unfilled Manpower and Health roles flagged since June, adding to the list PM Wong's next cabinet reshuffle will need to address, with no announced timeline yet.

singapore.headline: 13 CHARGED OVER FRAUDULENT SIM CARD SCHEME AS POLICE FLAG S$274,000 LOST TO "DIGIT-3" IMPERSONATION SCAMS
summary: Police said 13 people aged 19-31 will be charged between 20-24 July over their suspected involvement in a syndicate that paid subscribers S$10-30 per SIM card to sign up for and hand over multiple postpaid SIM cards, registered in their own names, to couriers — cards typically funnelled into scam operations.

Separately, police issued an advisory on a rising wave of government-official impersonation scams using unfamiliar eight-digit phone numbers beginning with "3": at least 12 victims have lost a combined S$274,000 since May, after being told (falsely) of suspicious transactions or misused identities, then transferred to a second scammer posing as a Ministry of Law, MAS or police official alleging money-laundering involvement.
singapore.geopolitical: Both schemes reflect syndicate-run fraud infrastructure that increasingly treats Singapore's clean regulatory reputation and trusted institutions — telcos, MAS, the Ministry of Law — as exploitable social-engineering assets rather than obstacles, a pattern regional law-enforcement cooperation has yet to fully disrupt at the recruitment layer.
singapore.socioeconomic: Cash-for-SIM-card recruitment preys on financially vulnerable subscribers for as little as S$10 a card, while the digit-3 scam's S$274,000 toll across just 12 known victims points to a high per-victim loss that continues to erode public trust in unsolicited calls even from numbers that superficially resemble legitimate contact formats.

singapore.headline: 481 FIRMS RECOGNISED AS "COMPANY OF GOOD" FOR NEARLY S$384 MILLION IN GIVING OVER 3 YEARS
summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong spoke at the Company of Good Conferment and Conference on Monday, where the National Volunteer & Philanthropy Centre recognised 481 organisations for embedding corporate purpose into their operations; the conferred companies collectively donated close to S$384 million over the past three years.
The figure builds on 2025's cohort of a then-record 393 companies (77% SMEs), suggesting continued growth in the decade-old Company of Good movement ahead of its 10th anniversary this year.
singapore.geopolitical: A growing corporate-giving movement gives Singapore a soft-power data point on regional ESG and philanthropy leadership, distinct from — and a useful counterweight to — the state-driven aid pledges (Ebola, earthquake relief) that have otherwise dominated Singapore's international giving headlines this year.
singapore.socioeconomic: Near-S$384 million in three-year corporate giving, with SMEs now a majority of conferees, suggests corporate philanthropy in Singapore is broadening beyond a handful of large givers even as households face their own cost-of-living pressures from record COE premiums and electricity tariffs.

singapore.headline: COMMUTER SURVEY FLAGS CROWDING, WAIT TIMES AND UNEVEN AIRCON AS TOP TRANSPORT GRIPES
summary: The Public Transport Council said Monday that its latest customer satisfaction survey of 5,505 commuters found 87% overall satisfaction, but identified crowding on buses and trains, irregular bus waiting times, and inconsistent air-conditioning on trains as the three areas commuters most want improved; courtesy and consideration among fellow commuters was flagged as a related concern from focus groups.
Commuters said they want more accurate, real-time arrival information to better plan journeys around irregular waits and crowded boarding, particularly on buses.
singapore.geopolitical: An 87% satisfaction score keeps Singapore's public transport system in the upper tier by regional comparison even as granular pain points persist — a useful contrast for policymakers weighing service levels against fare increases at a time transport systems across the region face sharper commuter backlash.
singapore.socioeconomic: Persistent crowding and wait-time complaints despite CCL6's recent opening and continued MRT reliability gains suggest capacity additions are running behind ridership growth, a planning gap that becomes more consequential as the RTS Link's 2027 opening reshapes cross-border commuting patterns.

word.definition: To express loud, vehement protest or criticism; archaically, to detonate or explode violently, as with thunder and lightning.
word.etymology: From Latin fulminare ("to strike with lightning"), from fulmen ("lightning bolt"), related to fulgere ("to flash, shine"); originally used of thunderbolts before extending metaphorically to verbal denunciations by the 16th century.
word.example: Trump fulminated against Canada on Truth Social before formalising a 50% tariff on its goods, even as Iran's president declared a "full-scale war" and Yemen's Houthis fulminated against Saudi Arabia with a new maritime embargo on the Red Sea.
